query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a rapid thermomechanical treatment (a severe plastic deformation step followed by a short-duration, high-rate annealing treatment) to a titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy will refine its microstructure and increase dislocation and grain boundary density, leading to enhanced yield strength and hardness under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment conditions relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state produced by conventional melting/homogenization.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to severe plastic deformation (such as cold rolling) followed by rapid annealing (using a high heating rate, e.g., >15 K/s, for a short duration) to produce an ultrafine-grained, highly dislocated microstructure while avoiding phase decomposition.
generation.conditions: Testing is conducted under elevated temperatures (typically 700°C to 900°C) or other extreme-environment conditions where high-temperature strength and structural stability are critical, and for compositions having Ti and Ni as primary constituents.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, ultrafine-grained microstructure with enhanced grain boundary density and an increased population of dislocations.
generation.mechanism: Grain boundary strengthening via the Hall–Petch effect combined with dislocation hardening. The refined microstructure resists high-temperature deformation and delays grain coarsening, thereby enhancing the elevated-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast or homogenized state, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield strength and hardness at elevated temperatures without introducing deleterious phase transformations.
generation.baseline: The titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy in its conventional single-phase, homogenized state without additional thermomechanical processing.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected as long as the rapid annealing treatment avoids triggering phase decomposition or excessive grain growth. The improvement is likely most significant below the temperature where these microstructural changes become unstable (roughly below 900°C) and for alloys designed with Ti and Ni as the main constituents.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative gains in mechanical properties and the long-term stability of the refined microstructure at high temperatures are uncertain and may depend on processing parameters (such as degree of deformation, annealing time, and heating rate).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy: one set is processed through the severe plastic deformation and rapid annealing route, and the other set is maintained in the as-cast/homogenized state. Subject both sets to mechanical testing (e.g., compressive and tensile tests) at elevated temperatures (700°C–900°C) alongside microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM and XRD) before and after testing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically treated specimens fail to consistently exhibit higher yield strength and hardness under elevated-temperature testing relative to the untreated control, or if significant adverse phase transformations or grain coarsening occurs, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Only the stabilization of chemical and phase composition, which took place after 100 h of homogenizing annealing, allowed for the determination of the relationship between changes in the grain size and changes in the hardness, and the conclusion that the produced material, despite the ultra-fine-grained granular structure, had a classic Hall–Petch relationship. Taking into account the time during which grain growth occurred and the associated slight decrease in hardness, it can be concluded that the alloys produced were characterized by high structural stability combined with the stability of the mechanical properties determined via hardness tests.

Over the last decades, the single-FCC or BCC HEAs have been intensively investigated and developed. In fact, it is very hard to reach a balance between high strength and high ductility for the single-phase HEAs due to the fact that the single-FCC HEAs normally have good ductility and poor strength, while the single-BCC HEAs generally have poor ductility and good strength. By adjusting the composition of the alloys, a eutectic high-entropy alloy AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with a regular FCC/BCC lamellar structure has been developed, and the alloy has an excellent combination of high strength and high ductility [], which was attributed to the coupling between the ductile FCC and brittle BCC phases during tension deformation []. A transformation-induced plasticity-assisted dual-phase (TRIP-DP) HEA has also been developed, in which two high-entropy phases (FCC γ matrix and laminate HCP ε phase) present []. The TRIP-DP HEA combines the solid-solution strengthening effect in HEAs with the TRIP effect, exhibits multiple deformation mechanisms and dynamic strain partitioning behavior [], and has improved strength and ductility compared to its corresponding single-phase HEA.
